findings.fix_hint: treat 404 as an idempotent success for cancel (e.g. include 404 in success_statuses or catch and return {}), or raise a distinct reason such as 'not_found' rather than 'unavailable'
findings.problem: cancel_download only accepts {200, 202, 204}. A cancel sent for a transfer slskd no longer knows about returns 404. That happens when the transfer already finished, was already removed, or raced with completion. _request_json then raises TransferEnqueueError("slskd transfer request failed with HTTP 404", "unavailable") at transfer.py:261. The result is the opposite of what a cancel caller wants: the desired end state (no active transfer) has been reached, but the call reports a service outage. A cancellation flow (the commit history shows active cancellation tests in progress, 22-03) will see a spurious 'unavailable' error and may mark the job as failed or retry instead of treating it as cancelled. pending: confirm slskd returns 404 for already-completed/removed transfer ids and how the upcoming pipeline caller handles this error (no production caller exists yet; only tests/test_jobs_api.py:520 stubs it).
findings.title: Cancel treats 404 (transfer already gone) as an 'unavailable' failure
findings.why_it_matters: A job-cancel flow that hits a transfer that just completed would report a slskd outage and could leave the job in a failed or retry state instead of cancelled.

findings.problem: cancel_download reuses _request_json, so a DELETE failure raises TransferEnqueueError. On 5xx, the reason comes from _classify_server_transfer_failure, which was written for enqueue responses (for example 'user_offline'). Callers that catch TransferEnqueueError around enqueue/poll logic (pipeline.py:924) could mistake a cancel failure for an enqueue failure and take enqueue-recovery paths such as switching to another candidate. pending: confirm how the cancel caller distinguishes cancel failures and what _classify_server_transfer_failure returns for a DELETE error body.
findings.title: Cancel 5xx errors classified with enqueue-specific failure logic and error type
findings.why_it_matters: A misleading error type or reason on cancel can send the pipeline down an enqueue-retry or candidate-fallback path during a user cancellation.

findings.fix_hint: use `success_statuses if success_statuses is not None else {200, 201}`
findings.problem: `success_statuses or {200, 201}` treats an explicitly passed empty set the same as None. No current caller passes an empty set, so this is latent: a future caller passing set() would get the default instead of 'nothing is success'.
findings.title: Empty success_statuses set silently falls back to {200, 201}
findings.why_it_matters: A small trap in the API contract. No impact today.

findings.problem: `success_statuses: set[int] | None = None` is resolved with `success_statuses or {200, 201}`. An empty set is falsy in Python, so a caller that explicitly passes `success_statuses=set()` (e.g. to mean "no status code is acceptable") would silently fall back to the default `{200, 201}` instead of rejecting every response. No current call site in this diff passes an empty set, so it has no live impact today, but the Optional is being treated as a truthiness check rather than an identity check against `None`.
findings.title: Optional set param collapsed to default via `or`, not `is None`
findings.why_it_matters: A future caller relying on an empty success set (deliberately strict) would get silently permissive default behavior instead of the intended rejection, and the bug would only surface at runtime under a code path nobody is currently exercising.
